description:
FOUND s502e (Opus, 2026-10-04) while shipping #2538 (Scalar::Util::set_prototype made real).  PRE-EXISTING on main e5d72352 and independent of #2538 (Sub::Util::set_prototype has the same gap).

REPRODUCER (scratch/s502e/p/sp2.pl in the s502e worktree; perl 5.40.3 first, PCL second):
    sub sp { scalar(@_) }
    my @l = (1, 2, 3);
    BEGIN { require Scalar::Util; Scalar::Util::set_prototype(\&sp, q($$)); }
    print "c ", sp(@l, 5), "\n";          # perl: c 2     PCL: c 4
    print "e ", eval q{ sp(@l, 5) }, "\n"; # perl: e 2     PCL: e 4

MECHANISM: PCL's prototype CONSUMPTION is a transpile-time fact (Pl::Environment's prototype table, filled from definitions and `use` merges); the run-time registry `%pcl-sub-prototypes` that set_prototype writes is read only by `prototype()`.  So a prototype installed at BEGIN time never reaches the parse of later statements, and a string eval (compiled at run time by the pl2cl server) does not consult the registry either.  prototype(\&sp) does answer '$$' (#2538).

CHEAP DISCRIMINATING MEASUREMENT for a fix: does the string-eval compile path receive any run-time prototype facts today?  grep the eval request builder in cl/pcl-runtime.lisp for what it sends besides the capture alist; if nothing, the eval half needs the registry's (name -> text) pairs for subs visible in the eval's package sent with the request (the same channel the capture names ride, #296-B1), and the file-level half needs BEGIN-time evaluation feeding the transpiler -- which PCL does not have (the compile phase runs after transpile).  The eval half is the reachable one.

POPULATION: rare in practice (set_prototype at BEGIN then a bareword call relying on it); recorded as residue (3) of the not-supported.md "prototype()" entry.


ADDED 2026-10-06 (Fable, from the PerlMonks 44722 probes, task #2774): the same family without set_prototype -- a sub DEFINED by a string eval in BEGIN.  `BEGIN { eval q{sub zzz () { 42 }} } print zzz / 2` prints 21 in perl and 0 in PCL (the name is not known when the file is parsed, so `zzz` in operator position is the string "zzz"; silent).  `BEGIN { *zzz = sub () { 42 } }` IS seen and prints 21; `zzz /foo/` with an eval-defined arg-taking sub is also right (unknown word + `/.../` is repaired to a call with a match).

ADDED same day: brian d foy's example from the same reddit thread -- `BEGIN { my $subname = 'do_it'; *{$subname} = COND ? sub ($) { "A: $_[0]" } : sub ($$) { "B: $_[0] \U$_[1]" }; }  say do_it 'a', 'b';` -- perl prints `A: ab` or `B: a B`; PCL is right in the ($$) branch and prints `A: a` in the ($) branch (both arguments go to do_it).  His `print rand 5, sin 4, rand sin 1, 2, 3;` is identical to perl.

=== s510 (Fable, 2026-10-06): A DETECTOR for this whole family -- design sketch, NOT built, NOT measured (USER: "can we recognize when we will fail because of that problem?") ===
The family: a sub, or a prototype, that only RUNNING code creates before later calls are parsed -- `*{$name} = COND ? sub ($) {...} : sub ($$) {...}` in BEGIN (foy), `BEGIN { eval(COND ? "sub zany ();" : "sub zany (@);") }` (merlyn, #2774's sibling), set_prototype in BEGIN (this task), `BEGIN { Module->import }` (#2053), a replaced built-in the compiler did not see (#2779 gap 2).  The compiler cannot know; the RUNTIME can, exactly, and before any mis-parsed call runs:
  1. the compiler writes into the emitted file, once per file, HOW IT PARSED each bareword call name: as the built-in NAME / as a call with prototype P / as a plain list call / as a string (an unknown word in operator position);
  2. the runtime has the places where a sub gets a name (`p-glob-assign`, `p-glob-assign-dynamic`, a `sub NAME` reached through a string eval, set_prototype) and knows whether the unit is still in its COMPILE phase (`*p-compile-phase-done*`);
  3. when a sub is installed or re-prototyped during the compile phase under a name in that table, and what it is (its prototype; or that it now displaces a built-in) differs from what the compiler assumed, the later calls WERE parsed wrongly: by rule 12 that is a tidy one-line DIE naming the sub, its prototype and the file (the wrong parse would have produced values) -- or an announcement, if the first measurement shows working programs tripping it.
Cost: nothing on any hot path (the check runs only when a sub is installed during a compile phase).  Known over-approximation: calls textually BEFORE the BEGIN block are parsed without the prototype by perl too, so the table needs line numbers to stay exact.  It would also turn today's SILENT wrong for import-generated constants (`use enum qw(A B)`-style modules that install `sub () {...}` at import: the file's bareword `A` is a string today) into a loud one.
FIRST MEASUREMENT before designing further: instrument the three install sites to LOG (not die) every compile-phase install whose prototype differs from the compiler's assumption, over the gate, the sweep, the everyday corpus and the CPAN board -- the count and the list of names decide die vs announce.

=== s510, later the same evening (Fable): the other possible answer, recorded as an IDEA ONLY -- ask real perl ===
brian d foy's objection on r/perl, in his words: "You don't know when it will be redefined ... The information is not fixed at the start of the compile-phase ... PPI tells you that you can't do this."  He also names PERL5OPT (not read by pcl: docs/not-supported.md, #2663; `pcl -MModule` works).
The transpiler itself runs under perl.  So at transpile time it COULD ask perl what the program's compile phase produces: `perl -c` on the program with a small module whose CHECK block dumps every package's subs and their prototypes (and which built-ins are displaced).  That would see BEGIN-time installs, `BEGIN { M->import }`, default exports, import-generated constants -- everything DETERMINISTIC.  What it costs, and why it is not proposed now: (1) the user's BEGIN blocks and every used module's body run at TRANSPILE time under perl -- side effects twice, the s509 exactly-once ruling's concern, and a program that needs its run-time environment to compile; (2) it gives the state at the END of the compile phase, not at each point of the parse (foy's "the first rand might differ from the next"); (3) it reads perl's REAL modules where PCL runs its own shims, whose prototypes are not guaranteed to match; (4) a coin-flip prototype (`time % 2`) stays unknowable to everyone.  The run-time detector above needs none of that and never runs user code early; this idea is here so nobody has to rediscover it.

=== s511 (Fable, 2026-10-07): THE CHEAP DISCRIMINATING MEASUREMENT IS TAKEN -- the eval compile receives NO prototype facts, run-time OR static ===
The request carries the text, the package, the capture NAMES and the features (the p-eval cache-key comment in cl/pcl-runtime.lisp); a plain `sub un3 ($)` in the MAIN FILE is already unknown to `eval q{un3 1, 2}` (perl u:1|2, PCL u:1).  So the eval half of this task is one instance of the wider gap, filed as #2870 with the fix channel (prototype pairs ride the request like the capture names and join the eval cache key); the BEGIN-time file half stays here with the detector sketch above.  Probes ~/pcl-agent-scratch/s511/review/eval-protos/.
subject: A prototype set at RUN time (Scalar/Sub::Util::set_prototype in BEGIN) is reported by prototype() but never changes how later calls parse -- incl. a string eval compiled after the set (perl sp(@l,5) passes 2 args, PCL 4)
